title: Pooja Sethi Wins Primary, One Step from Historic Texas House Seat
excerpt: The Indian American immigration attorney defeated a 20-year Army veteran for the Democratic nomination in Texas House District 47 and would be the first Indian American to serve in the Texas Legislature if she wins in November.
body:
• Pooja Sethi won the March Democratic primary for Texas House District 47 with 76% of the vote, defeating 20-year Army veteran Joseph Kopser.
  • The former chief of staff to outgoing Rep. Vikki Goodwin and immigration attorney with Catholic Charities is the first Indian American woman to run for a Texas House seat.
  • If she wins November's general election against Republican Jennifer Mushtaler, she would become the first Indian American — and the first Hindu — to serve in the Texas Legislature.
  • Her campaign was launched around gun violence after she stood beside a Uvalde shooting victim's father, and weathered a "Don't India my Texas" attack that was condemned by Asian American Democrats.

Pooja Sethi, an Indian American immigration attorney and former congressional aide, has won the Democratic primary for Texas House District 47 — a decisive victory that puts her one election away from becoming the first Indian American to serve in the Texas Legislature. Sethi defeated 20-year US Army veteran Joseph Kopser with 76.08% of the vote, 21,157 votes to Kopser's 6,653, according to election results.

A career built inside the building

Sethi is not a political outsider. She spent nearly four years as chief of staff to Texas State Representative Vikki Goodwin — the incumbent in District 47, who is retiring from the seat to run for lieutenant governor. Before the Capitol, Sethi worked as an immigration attorney with Catholic Charities, representing families navigating the immigration system. She also served as chair of the Travis County Democratic Party, and in 2021 the Texas House itself honored her with a resolution recognizing her help to neighbors during Winter Storm Uri.

Her community roots run deep in the Austin area she hopes to represent: past president of the Indian American Coalition of Central Texas, board service with the Austin Artists Project, Planned Parenthood Texas, Emerge Texas, the City of Austin's Asian American Quality of Life Commission and the ACC Regional Board. More than 150 elected officials and precinct chairs across Travis County endorsed her campaign, Lone Star Left reported.

Why she is running

Gun violence brought her into the race. "I'm running for Texas House District 47 because I'm a mom — and I cannot keep raising my child in a state that turns its back on kids," Sethi said, explaining that she had watched "cruelty win" session after session in the legislature. She described standing beside a father who lost his child in the Uvalde school shooting as he showed a House committee chair his child's school notebook — "with a bullet hole right through it" — while they sought a hearing on the "Raise the Age" bill, which would lift the minimum age to buy certain high-powered firearms from 18 to 21.

In a candidate questionnaire, she laid out a broad progressive platform: a $15 minimum wage, an end to tax subsidies for large corporations, opposition to school vouchers and charter schools, free school meals for all K-12 students, redirecting fossil-fuel subsidies toward community solar and battery projects, and ending funding for Operation Lone Star in favor of more immigration judges, case workers and border infrastructure.

The attack she weathered

The campaign was not without ugliness. Sethi was targeted with a "Don't India my Texas" attack — a line of insult aimed squarely at her heritage. The Asian American Democrats of Texas condemned it, saying such comments "are not political critiques or policy disagreements. They are rooted in fear and exclusion, and they send a message that some Texans do not belong."

Sethi's response, as reported by the Times of India, was defiant: her heritage was not the issue — the discomfort of others was. She won anyway, and decisively.

Context and background

District 47 covers western Travis County — Bee Cave, Lakeway and West Austin — and is a safe Democratic seat, with analysts describing Sethi as a strong favorite in November. The district's Asian population, at 14.6%, is more than double the statewide share of 6.3%, giving her background and community ties added resonance.

If she prevails against Republican nominee Jennifer Mushtaler in the November general election, the milestones would stack: the first Indian American woman to run for the Texas House would become the first Indian American, the first Hindu, and the first Asian Democratic woman ever to serve in the Texas Legislature.

"I'm running because I'm a mom — and I cannot keep raising my child in a state that turns its back on kids."

— Pooja Sethi, Democratic nominee for Texas House District 47

Diaspora angle

Sethi's candidacy is the latest milestone in the growing political footprint of Indian Americans in Texas — one of the largest and fastest-growing diaspora populations in the state. Her path, from Catholic Charities immigration attorney to Goodwin's chief of staff to nominee, is a case study in how diaspora professionals are converting community organizing and legislative staff work into electoral power.

What's next

The November general election will decide the seat, with Sethi considered the clear favorite in a safe blue district. Beyond her own race, her former boss Vikki Goodwin's bid for lieutenant governor means Texas voters will be watching the Indian American candidate pipeline closely. If Sethi wins, Austin's newest state representative will take her seat in the legislature in January 2027.
